l: State, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: A State may be preserved only by fortunate chance when its rulers lack principles and its ministers lack laws governing their duties. It is ruined when superiors disregard propriety and inferiors do not learn.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: The Book of Poetry is cited for teachings about following ancient statutes without transgression or forgetfulness. It is also cited as warning people not to remain at ease when the overthrow of Zhou is being produced by Heaven.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Benevolent government is necessary for the principles of Yao and Shun to secure the tranquil order of the kingdom. It arises from concern for human suffering and allows benevolence to overspread the kingdom.

l: government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Government requires both virtue and laws, since virtue alone cannot exercise it and laws cannot carry themselves into practice. It should proceed according to the ways of the former kings and be guided by concern for the sufferings of men.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Benevolence should be practiced through government rather than held only as a reputation or intention. When a benevolent person occupies a high station, benevolence can benefit those below and overspread the kingdom.

l: laws, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Laws alone cannot put themselves into practice, but following the laws of the ancient kings prevents error. Ministers need laws to remain in the discharge of their duties, and penal laws are violated when inferiors disregard proper order.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Rules of propriety govern how officials take office and retire from it and how superiors and inferiors conduct themselves. When superiors do not observe them and inferiors do not learn, seditious people arise and the State quickly perishes.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou) / Part I / Chapter 1
s: Righteousness is required of superiors in observing the laws and of officers in serving their prince. Officers who serve without righteousness or who reject the ways of the ancient kings are described as dilatory.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: Mencius says that the compass and square produce perfect circles and squares, while the sages perfectly exhibit human relations. He teaches that a sovereign should imitate Yao and a minister should imitate Shun in order to fulfill their duties. Confucius says that people have only two courses: virtue and its opposite. The text warns that a ruler who oppresses the people will be slain or endangered, and the kingdom will perish or be weakened; the Book of Poetry presents the downfall of Xia as a warning.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: Mencius says that the compass and square produce perfect circles and squares, and that the sages perfectly exhibit the human relations. He teaches that sovereigns should imitate Yao and ministers should imitate Shun in fulfilling their duties.

l: sages, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: The sages perfectly exhibit the human relations.

l: human relations, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: The human relations are perfectly exhibited by the sages.

l: sovereign, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: A sovereign should perfectly discharge the duties of a sovereign by imitating Yao. A sovereign who rules by severely oppressing the people will be slain, and a sovereign who stops short of the highest pitch of oppression will still endanger his life and weaken his kingdom.

l: Yao, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: Yao is presented as the model whom a sovereign should imitate. Yao ruled his people in a way that should be followed.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: Shun is presented as the model whom a minister should imitate. Shun served Yao in a way that demonstrates respect for a sovereign.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: Confucius says that there are only two courses that can be pursued: virtue and its opposite.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: Virtue is one of the two courses that can be pursued, according to Confucius.

l: its opposite, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: Its opposite is the other course that can be pursued, according to Confucius.

l: oppression, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: Oppression carried to the highest pitch causes a ruler to be slain and a kingdom to perish. Even oppression that stops short of the highest pitch places the ruler's life in danger and weakens the kingdom.

l: people, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: A ruler should rule the people as Yao ruled his. A ruler who carries oppression of the people to the highest pitch injures them.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: A kingdom perishes when its ruler carries oppression of the people to the highest pitch. If the oppression stops short of that pitch, the kingdom is weakened.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 2
s: The Book of Poetry says that the beacon of Yin is not remote and places it in the time of the last sovereign of Xia.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 3
s: Mencius explains that benevolence enabled the three dynasties to gain the throne, while failure to practice it caused them to lose the throne. He says that benevolence determines whether States and their rulers flourish, are preserved, decay, or perish. He warns that a sovereign who is not benevolent cannot keep the throne, and that a Head of a State who is not benevolent cannot preserve his rule.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 3
s: Mencius teaches that benevolence enabled the three dynasties to gain the throne and that lack of benevolence caused them to lose it. He explains that rulers and States cannot be preserved without benevolence.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 3
s: Benevolence determines the gaining and losing of the throne and the flourishing, preservation, decay, and perishing of States. A lack of benevolence prevents rulers and other people from preserving what they hold.

l: three dynasties, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 3
s: The three dynasties gained the throne through benevolence and lost it through not being benevolent.

l: the throne, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 3
s: The throne was gained by the three dynasties through benevolence and lost through a lack of benevolence. A sovereign cannot preserve the throne from passing away without benevolence.

l: States, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 3
s: The flourishing, preservation, decay, and perishing of States are determined by benevolence or its absence.

l: sovereign, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 3
s: A sovereign who is not benevolent cannot preserve the throne from passing from him.

l: Head of a State, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 3
s: A Head of a State who is not benevolent cannot preserve his rule.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: Mencius teaches that a person should examine himself when love, government, or politeness receives no responsive return. He says that when desires are not achieved through one's actions, one should examine oneself in every respect. He also says that when a man's person is correct, the whole kingdom will turn to him with recognition and submission. The Book of Poetry teaches that studying to harmonize with the ordinances of God brings much happiness.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: Mencius teaches that a person should turn inward and examine himself when his love, government, or politeness receives no responsive return.

l: man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: A man is told to examine his own benevolence, wisdom, and feeling of respect when his actions do not produce the desired response. When his person is correct, the whole kingdom will turn to him with recognition and submission.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: A man should examine his own benevolence when he loves others and no responsive attachment is shown to him.

l: government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: A man's government may be unsuccessful when he is trying to rule others, and he should then examine his wisdom.

l: wisdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: A man should examine his wisdom when his government is unsuccessful.

l: feeling of respect, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: A man should examine his own feeling of respect when he treats others politely and they do not return his politeness.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: When a man's person is correct, the whole kingdom will turn to him with recognition and submission.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: The Book of Poetry says that being always studious to be in harmony with the ordinances of God leads to much happiness.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 4
s: The ordinances of God are presented as something with which a person should be in harmony in order to obtain much happiness.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 5
s: Mencius states that people commonly speak of the kingdom, the State, and the family. He explains that the State is the root of the kingdom. He further explains that the family is the root of the State, and the person of its Head is the root of the family.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 5
s: Mencius states that people commonly speak of the kingdom, the State, and the family. He explains the roots connecting these three levels.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 5
s: The kingdom has the State as its root.

l: State, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 5
s: The State has the family as its root.

l: family, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 5
s: The family has the person of its Head as its root.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 6
s: Mencius says that the administration of government is not difficult when it avoids offending the great families. The influence of the great families extends through the whole State, and the influence of any one State extends through the whole kingdom. When this influence operates, a person's virtue and teachings spread throughout the four seas like rushing water.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 6
s: Mencius says that the administration of government is not difficult if it does not offend the great families.

l: administration of government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 6
s: The administration of government is described as not difficult when it avoids offending the great families.

l: great families, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 6
s: The great families affect the whole State, so whoever they affect will be affected by the whole State.

l: State, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 6
s: The whole State affects whoever any of the great families affect.

l: State (any one State), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 6
s: Any one State affects whoever it affects throughout the whole kingdom.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 6
s: The whole kingdom is affected by whoever any one State affects.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius explains that under right government, princes of little virtue or worth submit to those of greater virtue or worth, while under bad government, weaker princes submit to stronger ones. He identifies both patterns as the rule of Heaven, saying those who accord with Heaven are preserved and those who rebel against it perish. He advises small States that are ashamed to receive commands to imitate king Wen, after which they may give laws to the kingdom within five or seven years. He concludes that a prince who loves benevolence will have no opponent in the kingdom, but seeking that result without benevolence is like handling a heated substance without first dipping it in water.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius explains how princes submit to one another under right government and bad government. He advises a prince who is ashamed to receive commands to imitate king Wen and teaches that benevolence removes opposition.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: Heaven establishes both the submission of lesser princes to greater ones under right government and the submission of weaker princes to stronger ones under bad government. Those who accord with Heaven are preserved, while those who rebel against it perish.

l: right government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: Right government causes princes of little virtue to submit to those of great virtue and princes of little worth to those of great worth.

l: bad government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: Bad government causes princes of small power to submit to those of great power and the weak to submit to the strong.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: The kingdom is governed by patterns of submission among princes. A prince who loves benevolence can have no opponent throughout the kingdom and may eventually give laws to it.

l: princes, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: Princes of little virtue or worth submit to those of greater virtue or worth when right government prevails. Under bad government, princes of small power and the weak submit to those who are stronger.

l: small States, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: Small States imitate large States but are ashamed to receive their commands. They are compared to a scholar who is ashamed to receive the commands of his master.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: King Wen is presented as the model for a prince who is ashamed to receive commands. Imitating king Wen is said to enable a large State to give laws to the kingdom in five years and a small State in seven years.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 7
s: Benevolence gives a prince no opponent in the kingdom. Seeking that result without being benevolent is compared to handling a heated substance without first dipping it in water.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: Mencius questions how anyone can speak with princes who are not benevolent and who mistake dangers and calamities for safety and profit. A boy’s song about the water of the Cang Lang leads Confucius to explain that its different applications depend on whether the water is clear or muddy. The unit teaches that a man, family, or State first brings about its own disgrace or destruction before others do so. It concludes that Heaven-sent calamities may be escaped, but self-caused calamities cannot be survived.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: Mencius asks how it is possible to speak with princes who are not benevolent. He connects their destructive condition with counting perils as safety, calamities as profitable, and taking pleasure in what causes their ruin.

l: princes, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: The princes described are not benevolent and treat perils as safety and calamities as profitable. Their conduct leads toward the destruction of States and the ruin of Families.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: Benevolence is violated by princes who take pleasure in things by which they perish. The text presents such violation as making productive discussion with them impossible.

l: calamities, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: Calamities may be sent down by Heaven and can still be escaped. Calamities occasioned by people themselves cannot be escaped or survived.

l: States, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: States are destroyed when they first smite themselves, after which others will smite them. Princes who are not benevolent are associated with the destruction of States.

l: Families, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: Families are ruined when they first destroy themselves, after which others will destroy them. Their ruin is linked with the conduct of princes who are not benevolent.

l: water of the Cang Lang, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: The water of the Cang Lang is sung of as washing the strings of a cap when it is clear and washing the feet when it is muddy. Its different applications illustrate that the water’s condition determines how it is used.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: Confucius tells his children to hear the boy’s song about the water of the Cang Lang. He explains that clear water is used for cap-strings and muddy water for washing feet.

l: man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: A man must first despise himself before others will despise him. His own conduct is presented as preceding the contempt he receives from others.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 8
s: Heaven can send down calamities that are still possible to escape. The text contrasts these with calamities people occasion themselves, which cannot be escaped.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: Mencius explains that Jie and Zhou lost the throne because they lost the people and their hearts. He says that rulers can gain the kingdom by gaining the people, whose hearts are won by providing what they like and avoiding what they dislike. The people turn toward a benevolent rule, while Jie and Zhou unintentionally drove them toward Tang and Wu. Mencius urges the present rulers of the kingdom to set their wills on benevolence or face sorrow, disgrace, death, and ruin.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: Mencius teaches that Jie and Zhou lost the throne by losing the people and their hearts. He says that rulers must gain the people through benevolence, by providing what they like and avoiding what they dislike.

l: Jie, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: Jie lost the throne by losing the people and their hearts. Jie aided Tang by driving the people toward him.

l: Zhou, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: Zhou lost the throne by losing the people and their hearts. Zhou aided Wu by driving the people toward him.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: Tang was aided by Jie, whose actions drove the people toward Tang.

l: Wu, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: Wu was aided by Zhou, whose actions drove the people toward Wu.

l: people, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: The people are gained when their hearts are gained, which requires collecting what they like and not imposing what they dislike. The people turn toward a benevolent rule as water flows downward and wild beasts fly to the wilderness.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: The kingdom is gained by gaining the people. A ruler who loves benevolence would become sovereign because the other princes would drive the people toward him.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: A benevolent rule attracts the people, who turn toward it as water flows downward and wild beasts fly to the wilderness.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: Benevolence is presented as necessary for rulers who want to gain the people and the kingdom. Princes who do not set their wills on benevolence face sorrow, disgrace, death, and ruin.

l: the present rulers of the kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: The present rulers of the kingdom are warned that loving benevolence would cause the other princes to aid them by driving the people toward them. If they do not set their wills on benevolence, they will remain in sorrow and disgrace and become involved in death and ruin.

l: the other princes, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 9
s: The other princes would aid any present ruler who loved benevolence by driving the people toward that ruler.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 10
s: Mencius says that it is impossible to speak with those who do violence to themselves or to do anything with those who throw themselves away. He defines doing violence to oneself as rejecting propriety and righteousness in conversation. He defines throwing oneself away as claiming an inability to dwell in benevolence or pursue the path of righteousness. He teaches that benevolence is man's tranquil habitation and righteousness is his straight path, lamenting those who abandon both.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 10
s: Mencius says that it is impossible to speak with those who do violence to themselves or to do anything with those who throw themselves away. He defines benevolence as the tranquil habitation of man and righteousness as his straight path.

l: those who do violence to themselves, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 10
s: Those who do violence to themselves disown propriety and righteousness in their conversation. Mencius says it is impossible to speak with them.

l: those who throw themselves away, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 10
s: Those who throw themselves away say they are unable to dwell in benevolence or pursue the path of righteousness. Mencius says it is impossible to do anything with them.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 10
s: Benevolence is described as the tranquil habitation of man. Those who throw themselves away say they cannot dwell in it.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 10
s: Righteousness is described as man's straight path. Those who do violence to themselves disown it in conversation, while those who throw themselves away say they cannot pursue it.

l: the path of righteousness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 10
s: The path of righteousness is something that those who throw themselves away claim they cannot pursue.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 11
s: Mencius explains that the path of duty is found in what is near, but men seek it in what is remote. He says the work of duty is found in what is easy, but men seek it in what is difficult. He teaches that if each man loves his parents and shows due respect to his elders, the whole land would enjoy tranquillity.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 11
s: Mencius says that the path of duty lies in what is near and that its work lies in what is easy. He teaches that loving parents and showing due respect to elders would bring tranquillity to the whole land.

l: duty, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 11
s: Duty has a path that lies in what is near. Its work lies in what is easy, although men seek both in what is remote or difficult.

l: men, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 11
s: Men seek the path of duty in what is remote and its work in what is difficult. Each man is urged to love his parents and show due respect to his elders.

l: parents, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 11
s: Parents are to be loved by each man.

l: elders, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 11
s: Elders are to receive due respect from each man.

l: feeling of respect, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 11
s: Respect is to be shown duly to elders.

l: the whole land, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 11
s: The whole land would enjoy tranquillity if each man loved his parents and showed due respect to his elders.

l: tranquillity, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 11
s: Tranquillity would be enjoyed by the whole land if each man loved his parents and showed due respect to his elders.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 12
s: Mencius explains how those occupying inferior situations can succeed in governing the people by obtaining the confidence of the sovereign. He connects that confidence to being trusted by friends, serving parents so as to please them, and possessing inward sincerity. He teaches that sincerity depends on understanding what is good and calls sincerity the way of Heaven. He also states that complete sincerity moves others, while its absence prevents a person from moving others.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 12
s: Mencius explains the conditions by which those occupying inferior situations can obtain the confidence of the sovereign and succeed in governing the people. He teaches that sincerity is the way of Heaven and that complete sincerity moves others.

l: those occupying inferior situations, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 12
s: Those occupying inferior situations cannot succeed in governing the people unless they obtain the confidence of the sovereign.

l: sovereign, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 12
s: The sovereign's confidence must be obtained by those occupying inferior situations if they are to succeed in governing the people. That confidence depends on being trusted by friends.

l: people, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 12
s: The people cannot be successfully governed by those occupying inferior situations unless those persons obtain the confidence of the sovereign.

l: friends, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 12
s: Friends trust a person who serves his parents so as to make them pleased. A person who is not trusted by his friends will not obtain the confidence of the sovereign.

l: parents, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 12
s: Parents are pleased when a person serves them sincerely. A person who finds a want of sincerity on turning his thoughts inward will not give pleasure to his parents.

l: sincerity, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 12
s: Sincerity is attained through understanding what is good and is described as the way of Heaven. Complete sincerity moves others, while a person without sincerity cannot move others.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 12
s: Heaven is associated with sincerity, which is called the way of Heaven.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 13
s: Mencius recounts how Bo Yi and Tai Gong, while avoiding Zhou, lived on the northern and eastern coasts respectively. After hearing of the rise of king Wen, both decided to follow him because they had heard that the chief of the West knew how to nourish the old. Their allegiance represented the fathers of the kingdom joining king Wen, which would draw the sons to him as well. Mencius says that any prince who practiced the government of king Wen would within seven years be giving laws to the kingdom.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 13
s: Mencius recounts the actions of Bo Yi and Tai Gong and explains the significance of their following king Wen. He says that a prince practicing the government of king Wen would within seven years be giving laws to the kingdom.

l: Bo Yi, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 13
s: Bo Yi lived on the coast of the northern sea while avoiding Zhou. When he heard of the rise of king Wen, he decided to follow him because he had heard that the chief of the West knew how to nourish the old.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 13
s: King Wen's rise caused Bo Yi and Tai Gong to decide to follow him. Their joining him represented the fathers of the kingdom coming to follow him.

l: Tai Gong, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 13
s: Tai Gong lived on the coast of the eastern sea while avoiding Zhou. When he heard of the rise of king Wen, he decided to follow him because he had heard that the chief of the West knew how to nourish the old.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 13
s: The kingdom's fathers joined king Wen when Bo Yi and Tai Gong followed him, and the kingdom's sons would then have no reason to go to anyone else. Any prince who practiced the government of king Wen would within seven years be giving laws to the kingdom.

l: government of king Wen, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 13
s: The government of king Wen is presented as a form of government that, if practiced by any prince, would lead to that prince giving laws to the kingdom within seven years.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Mencius discusses Qiu, who served the head of the Ji family but failed to change his evil ways and exacted double grain from the people. Confucius rejected Qiu as a disciple and called for him to be attacked. The passage condemns ministers who enrich princes, especially those who fight for them and cause mass slaughter. It ranks skilful fighters, league-makers, and those who seize grassy commons for punishment, with the first suffering the highest punishment.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Mencius recounts Qiu's service to the head of the Ji family and examines how ministers who enrich rulers should be judged.

l: Qiu, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Qiu acted as chief officer to the head of the Ji family, failed to change his evil ways, and exacted double the grain formerly paid from the people. Confucius rejected him as a disciple and called for him to be attacked.

l: Ji family, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: The Ji family had a head whom Qiu served as chief officer. Its head is described as practising evil ways.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Confucius rejected ministers who enriched princes when those princes did not practise benevolent government. He rejected Qiu as a disciple and called for him to be attacked.

l: people, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: The people were made to pay double the grain formerly paid by Qiu. They could also be compelled to cultivate ground taken into grassy commons.

l: ministers, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Ministers who enriched a prince who was not practising benevolent government were rejected by Confucius. Ministers who fought vehemently for their prince were viewed as even more deserving of rejection.

l: princes, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Princes who did not practise benevolent government could be enriched by ministers whom Confucius rejected. Some princes were joined in leagues against other princes.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Benevolent government is presented as a standard that princes may fail to practise. Ministers who enrich a prince lacking it are rejected by Confucius.

l: contentions about territory, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Contentions about territory can become the ground on which fighting occurs. When this happens, men are slaughtered until the fields are filled with them.

l: territory, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Territory can be the cause of contentions that lead princes or their forces to fight and slaughter men.

l: struggle for a city, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: A struggle for a city can be the ground on which fighting occurs. When this happens, men are slaughtered until the city is filled with them.

l: city, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: A city can become the object of a struggle in which men are slaughtered until the city is filled with them.

l: land, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Land is described as being led to devour human flesh when fighting over territory or cities fills fields and cities with slaughtered men.

l: such a crime, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Such a crime is the slaughter caused by fighting over territory or cities and is said to deserve more than death as a penalty.

l: punishment, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 14
s: Those skilful at fighting should suffer the highest punishment. Next should be those who unite princes in leagues against others, followed by those who take in grassy commons and impose cultivation on the people.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 15
s: Mencius teaches that the pupil of the eye is the most excellent part of a man's body. The pupil cannot hide a man's wickedness because it is bright when his breast is correct and dull when it is not. By listening to a man's words and looking at his pupil, one can learn his character.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 15
s: Mencius teaches that the pupil of the eye reveals whether a man's breast is correct. He says that a man's words and pupil together disclose his character.

l: man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 15
s: A man cannot use his pupil to hide his wickedness. His pupil is bright when all within his breast is correct and dull when it is not.

l: character, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 15
s: A man's character can be learned by listening to his words and looking at the pupil of his eye.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 16
s: Mencius explains that respectful people do not despise others and economical people do not plunder them. He says a prince who despises and plunders people is merely afraid they will not obey him. Mencius questions whether respectfulness and economy can be shown only through vocal tones and a smiling manner.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 16
s: Mencius teaches that the respectful do not despise others and the economical do not plunder them. He argues that a prince who despises and plunders people is motivated by fear that they will not obey him, and he questions whether respectfulness and economy can come from tones of voice and a smiling manner.

l: the respectful, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 16
s: The respectful do not despise others.

l: the economical, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 16
s: The economical do not plunder others.

l: prince, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 16
s: A prince who treats people with despite and plunders them is afraid that they may not prove obedient to him. Such a prince cannot be regarded as respectful or economical.

l: people, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 16
s: People may be despised or plundered by a prince who fears they will not obey him. They are also the others whom the respectful do not despise and the economical do not plunder.

l: respectfulness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 16
s: Respectfulness is associated with not despising others. Mencius questions whether it can be made out of tones of the voice and a smiling manner.

l: economy, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 16
s: Economy is associated with not plundering others. Mencius questions whether it can be made out of tones of the voice and a smiling manner.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 17
s: Chun Yu Kun asks Mencius whether males and females should avoid touching hands when giving or receiving things. Mencius says this is the general rule but explains that a man must rescue his drowning sister-in-law with his hand. Kun compares the whole kingdom to a drowning person and questions why Mencius will not rescue it. Mencius answers that a drowning kingdom must be rescued with right principles, not by hand.

l: Chun Yu Kun, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 17
s: Chun Yu Kun asks Mencius about the rule against males and females touching hands. He challenges Mencius by saying that the whole kingdom is drowning and asking why Mencius will not rescue it.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 17
s: Mencius states that males and females should not allow their hands to touch in giving and receiving as a general rule. He says a man who would not rescue his drowning sister-in-law with his hand is a wolf, and that a drowning kingdom must be rescued with right principles.

l: the rule, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 17
s: The rule is that males and females shall not allow their hands to touch in giving or receiving anything. Mencius describes it as the general rule, subject to a peculiar exigency such as rescuing a drowning sister-in-law.

l: sister-in-law (the man's sister-in-law), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 17
s: The man's sister-in-law is presented as drowning. Mencius says she must be rescued with the hand despite the general rule.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 17
s: The whole kingdom is described by Chun Yu Kun as drowning. Mencius says it must be rescued with right principles.

l: rescue, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 17
s: Rescue of a drowning sister-in-law requires taking her hand. Rescue of a drowning kingdom requires right principles rather than a hand.

l: right principles, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 17
s: Right principles are identified by Mencius as the means by which a drowning kingdom must be rescued.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 18
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius why the superior man does not personally teach his son. Mencius explains that a teacher must give correct instruction, but anger and reproving admonitions can cause father and son to become offended with each other. He says the ancients exchanged sons for teaching because alienation between father and son is especially inauspicious.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 18
s: Gong Sun Chou asks why the superior man does not himself teach his son.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 18
s: Mencius explains that the circumstances make it unsuitable for a father to teach his own son. He says that anger over unpractised lessons can offend both father and son, and that the ancients therefore exchanged sons for teaching.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 18
s: The superior man is described as not personally teaching his son because the circumstances of the relationship forbid it.

l: son (the superior man's son), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 18
s: The son receives instruction from his father but may fail to practise it. He can become offended when his father responds with anger or reproving admonitions.

l: teacher (the father), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 18
s: The teacher, who is the father, must inculcate what is correct. If the lessons are not practised, he may become angry and be offended with his son.

l: pupil (the son), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 18
s: The pupil, who is the son, observes that his master teaches what is correct but does not himself proceed in a correct path. This contributes to offense between the pupil and his father.

l: correct instruction, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 18
s: Correct instruction is what the teacher must inculcate. When it is not practised, following it up with anger can produce offense and alienation.

l: alienation, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 18
s: Alienation can arise when father and son exchange reproving admonitions. It is described as especially inauspicious between them.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: Mencius teaches that serving parents is the greatest service and taking charge of oneself is the greatest charge. He says that those who preserve themselves can serve their parents, and that service of parents and charge of oneself are roots of other duties. The examples of Zengzi and Zeng Yuan distinguish nourishing a parent’s will from merely nourishing the mouth and body. Serving parents as Zengzi served his is presented as filial piety.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: Mencius says that the service of parents is the greatest service and the charge of oneself is the greatest charge. He teaches that preserving oneself enables service to parents and that these duties are roots of other services and charges.

l: Zengzi, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: Zengzi nourishes his father, Zeng Xi, by providing wine and flesh and asking respectfully to whom the leftovers should be given. His practice is called nourishing the will, and serving parents in this way may be accepted as filial piety.

l: Zeng Xi, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: Zeng Xi is nourished by Zengzi, who provides wine and flesh and respectfully asks about distributing what remains. When Zeng Xi asks whether anything is left, Zengzi says that there is.

l: Zeng Yuan, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: Zeng Yuan nourishes his father, Zengzi, by providing wine and flesh. He does not ask to whom the leftovers should be given and says there is nothing left when asked, intending to bring the food in again.

l: parents, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: Parents are the recipients of the greatest service. The text says that serving parents is the root of all other services.

l: self, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: The self is the object of the greatest charge. The text says that those who do not fail to keep themselves can serve their parents.

l: service of one's parents, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: The service of parents is described as the greatest service and the root of all other services. Serving parents as Zengzi served his father may be accepted as filial piety.

l: charge of one's self, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: The charge of one's self is described as the greatest charge and the root of all other charges. Keeping oneself enables a person to serve their parents.

l: nourishing the mouth and body, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: Nourishing the mouth and body is the name given to Zeng Yuan's practice of providing wine and flesh while intending to bring leftovers in again. It contrasts with nourishing the will.

l: nourishing the will, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: Nourishing the will is the name given to Zengzi's practice of respectfully asking to whom leftover wine and flesh should be given. It concerns serving a parent in the manner described as filial piety.

l: great filial piety, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 19
s: Filial piety may be accepted when a person serves their parents as Zengzi served his father. The text connects it with nourishing the will.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 20
s: Mencius says that remonstrating with a sovereign about the mal-employment of ministers or blaming errors of government is not enough. He says only the great man can rectify what is wrong in the sovereign's mind. If the prince is benevolent, righteous, and correct, his acts and everything under him will reflect those qualities, and once the ruler is rectified, the kingdom will be firmly settled.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 20
s: Mencius teaches that remonstrating with a sovereign about the mal-employment of ministers or blaming errors of government is insufficient. He says that only the great man can rectify what is wrong in the sovereign's mind.

l: sovereign, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 20
s: The sovereign should have what is wrong in his mind rectified. His character determines whether his acts are benevolent, righteous, and correct.

l: great man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 20
s: The great man is the one who can rectify what is wrong in the sovereign's mind.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 20
s: Benevolence in the prince causes all his acts to be benevolent.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 20
s: Righteousness in the prince causes all his acts to be righteous.

l: correctness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 20
s: Correctness in the prince causes everything to be correct.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 20
s: The kingdom will be firmly settled once the ruler is rectified.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 21
s: Chapter 21 records a statement by Mencius. Mencius says that some praise cannot be expected. He also says that reproach can occur when the parties involved have been seeking to be perfect.

l: Chapter 21, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 21
s: Chapter 21 contains a statement by Mencius about unexpected praise and reproach directed at parties seeking to be perfect.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 21
s: Mencius says that there are cases of praise which could not be expected, and of reproach when the parties have been seeking to be perfect.

l: praise, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 21
s: Praise can occur in cases where it could not have been expected.

l: reproach, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 21
s: Reproach can occur when the parties have been seeking to be perfect.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 22
s: Mencius explains why men are ready with their tongues. He says this readiness arises simply because they have not been reproved. The unit concerns the relationship between men's readiness with their tongues and the absence of reproof.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 22
s: Mencius says that men's readiness with their tongues arises from not having been reproved.

l: men, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 22
s: Men are described as being ready with their tongues when they have not been reproved.

l: readiness with their tongues, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 22
s: Readiness with their tongues arises simply from men not having been reproved.

l: reproof, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 22
s: The absence of reproof is presented as the cause of men's readiness with their tongues.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 23
s: Mencius comments on the evil of men. He says that men like to be teachers of others. The unit concerns men, their evil, and their attitude toward teaching others.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 23
s: Mencius says that the evil of men is that they like to be teachers of others.

l: men, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 23
s: Men are described as liking to be teachers of others.

l: evil, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 23
s: The evil of men is identified as their liking to be teachers of others.

l: teachers, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 23
s: Teachers are presented as a role that men like to assume toward others.

l: others, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 23
s: Others are the people whom men like to teach.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 24
s: Yue Zheng traveled to Qi and came to see Mencius. Mencius questioned whether Yue Zheng had come specifically to see him and learned that Yue Zheng had arrived the previous day. Yue Zheng explained that his lodging-house had not been arranged. Mencius taught that a scholar's lodging-house should be arranged before visiting an elder, and Yue Zheng admitted that he had done wrong.

l: Yue Zheng, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 24
s: Yue Zheng went to Qi and came to see Mencius. He said that his lodging-house had not been arranged and admitted that he had done wrong.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 24
s: Mencius questioned Yue Zheng about his visit and arrival. He taught that a scholar's lodging-house must be arranged before he visits his elder.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 24
s: Qi was the destination to which Yue Zheng traveled.

l: Yue Zheng's visit to Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 24
s: Yue Zheng came to see Mencius after arriving in Qi the previous day. Mencius questioned the timing and circumstances of the visit.

l: lodging-house, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 24
s: Yue Zheng's lodging-house had not been arranged when he came to see Mencius.

l: proper lodging arrangements before visiting an elder, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 24
s: Mencius stated that a scholar's lodging-house must be arranged before the scholar visits his elder. Yue Zheng acknowledged that failing to do this was wrong.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 25
s: Mencius addresses the disciple Yue Zheng about his coming there in the train of Zi Ao. Mencius says that Yue Zheng came only because of the food and drink. He expresses disbelief that Yue Zheng, having learned the doctrine of the ancients, would act with a view to eating and drinking.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 25
s: Mencius addresses Yue Zheng and reproaches him for coming in the train of Zi Ao only for food and drink. He says he could not have thought that Yue Zheng would act with a view to eating and drinking after learning the doctrine of the ancients.

l: Yue Zheng, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 25
s: Yue Zheng is addressed by Mencius as having come in the train of Zi Ao only because of the food and drink. He is described as having learned the doctrine of the ancients, yet acting with a view to eating and drinking.

l: food and drink, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 25
s: Food and drink are identified by Mencius as the reason Yue Zheng came in the train of Zi Ao.

l: doctrine of the ancients, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 25
s: The doctrine of the ancients is something Yue Zheng has learned. Mencius says he did not expect Yue Zheng to act with a view to eating and drinking after learning it.

l: coming here in the train of Zi Ao, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 25
s: Coming here in the train of Zi Ao is described by Mencius as something Yue Zheng did only because of the food and drink.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 26
s: Mencius identifies three things as unfilial and says that having no posterity is the greatest. Shun married without informing his parents because he feared having no posterity. Superior men judge that Shun’s action was equivalent to informing his parents.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 26
s: Mencius says that there are three things which are unfilial, with having no posterity as the greatest.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 26
s: Shun married without informing his parents because he feared having no posterity. Superior men consider his action equivalent to informing them.

l: three unfilial things, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 26
s: The three unfilial things are mentioned, but the text identifies only having no posterity as the greatest among them.

l: posterity (Shun's posterity), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 26
s: Having no posterity is described as the greatest of the three unfilial things. Shun married because he feared having no posterity.

l: parents (Shun's parents), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 26
s: Shun married without informing his parents. Superior men consider that action equivalent to informing them.

l: Shun's marriage, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 26
s: Shun's marriage took place without his informing his parents, because he feared having no posterity.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Mencius describes the richest fruits of benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, propriety, and music. Benevolence is fulfilled in the service of one's parents, while righteousness is fulfilled in obeying one's elder brothers. Wisdom knows these two things and does not depart from them; propriety orders and adorns them; music rejoices in them, causing them to grow until joy is expressed through dancing feet and moving hands.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Mencius says that the richest fruits of benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, propriety, and music are found in relation to serving one's parents and obeying one's elder brothers.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Benevolence bears its richest fruit in the service of one's parents.

l: service of one's parents, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: The service of one's parents is identified as the richest fruit of benevolence.

l: parents, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Parents are the ones served in the richest fruit of benevolence.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Righteousness bears its richest fruit in obeying one's elder brothers.

l: obeying one's elder brothers, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Obeying one's elder brothers is identified as the richest fruit of righteousness.

l: elder brothers, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Elder brothers are the ones obeyed in the richest fruit of righteousness.

l: wisdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Wisdom consists in knowing the service of one's parents and the obeying of one's elder brothers, and not departing from them.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Propriety consists in ordering and adorning the service of one's parents and the obeying of one's elder brothers.

l: music, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Music consists in rejoicing in the service of one's parents and the obeying of one's elder brothers. When they are rejoiced in, they grow, and joy eventually causes the feet to dance and the hands to move.

l: rejoicing in those two things, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 27
s: Rejoicing in the service of one's parents and the obeying of one's elder brothers causes them to grow. When this rejoicing cannot be repressed, the feet begin to dance and the hands to move unconsciously.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 28
s: Mencius describes Shun as uniquely able to regard the whole kingdom’s joyful submission as insignificant compared with gaining his parents’ hearts. Shun fully served his father, Gu Sou, until Gu Sou found delight in what was good. Gu Sou’s change transformed the kingdom, establishing proper duties between fathers and sons, which is called great filial piety.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 28
s: Shun regarded gaining the whole kingdom’s joyful submission as no more than a bundle of grass. He believed that a person could not be considered a man without gaining his parents’ hearts or a son without reaching complete accord with them, and he fully served Gu Sou until Gu Sou found delight in what was good.

l: Gu Sou, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 28
s: Gu Sou was brought by Shun’s complete service to find delight in what was good. His change transformed the kingdom and established fathers and sons in their respective duties.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 28
s: The whole kingdom turned in great delight to submit to an individual, but Shun regarded this as insignificant. When Gu Sou found delight in what was good, the kingdom was transformed and fathers and sons were established in their respective duties.

l: delight, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 28
s: Delight describes the whole kingdom’s joyful submission to an individual and Gu Sou’s enjoyment of what was good. Gu Sou’s delight brought about the transformation of the whole kingdom.

l: great filial piety, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Chapter 28
s: Great filial piety is the condition in which a person completely fulfills everything by which a parent can be served, brings the parent to find delight in what is good, and thereby establishes proper duties throughout the kingdom.

l: Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: Mencius discusses the conduct of sages, rulers, ministers, scholars, and superior men. He explains how benevolence, righteousness, propriety, learning, self-examination, and steadfast conduct should guide people. Confucius is mentioned for his judgments, praise of exemplary conduct, and teaching that sages are like other men. The final story condemns deceptive pursuit of riches, honours, gain, and advancement.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: Mencius compares the principles of Shun and King Wen, criticizes rulers who try to please everyone, and explains proper treatment of ministers. He teaches that people should act with benevolence, righteousness, propriety, self-examination, and resolve, and comments on Confucius, Yu, Ji, Yan Hui, and others.

l: Middle Kingdom, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: The Middle Kingdom is the realm in which Shun and King Wen carried their principles into practice after obtaining what they wished.

l: Chun Qiu, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: The Chun Qiu was produced after sovereign rule's traces were extinguished and the royal odes ceased. Mencius says its subject was the affairs of Huan of Qi and Wen of Jin, and that Confucius made its righteous decisions.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: Confucius praised Yu, Ji, and Yan Hui for their conduct. He is also quoted as saying that the righteous decisions in the Chun Qiu were ones he ventured to make.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: Benevolence involves loving others and nourishing people through excellence. Mencius says a person should examine himself for a lack of benevolence and become especially benevolent when treated perversely.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: Righteousness is a path followed by Shun and a principle that should guide conduct. Acts that are not truly righteous are rejected by the great man.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: Propriety involves showing respect to others and following prescribed rules. The superior man examines himself for a lack of propriety and continues to observe it even when others behave unreasonably.

l: great man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: The great man does not perform acts of propriety or righteousness that are not genuinely proper or righteous. He speaks and acts rightly without planning beforehand to appear sincere or resolute, and he does not lose his child's-heart.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book IV (Li Lou), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 33
s: The superior man learns deeply and by the proper course, internalizes what he learns, and relies on it firmly. He preserves benevolence and propriety, examines himself when others act wrongly, and is concerned with becoming like Shun rather than with temporary calamity.

l: Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Mencius answers Wan Zhang’s questions about Shun’s filial conduct, marriage, accession, treatment of Xiang, and relationship with Gu Sou. He explains that Heaven and the people accepted Shun through his conduct, and that succession depended on Heaven’s ordinance rather than personal appointment. Mencius contrasts the successions of Shun, Yu, Yi, and Qi, explaining why Qi succeeded Yu’s son while Yi did not receive the throne. He also explains that Yi Yin approached Tang through the principles of Yao and Shun, urging Tang to attack Xia and save its people.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Mencius explains to Wan Zhang why Shun wept over his parents, why Shun married without informing them, and why Shun treated Xiang with affection. He teaches that Heaven showed its will through Shun’s conduct and the people’s acceptance, and he describes the principles governing succession and Yi Yin’s service to Tang.

l: Wan Zhang, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Wan Zhang asks Mencius about Shun’s sorrow, marriage, treatment of Xiang, accession, succession, and Yi Yin’s introduction to Tang. His questions lead Mencius to explain filial piety, Heaven’s mandate, and righteous government.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Shun wept because, despite receiving beauty, wealth, honours, and the kingdom’s approval, he lacked the accord of his parents. He married without informing his parents because informing them would have prevented the marriage, and he sincerely welcomed Xiang despite knowing Xiang had sought to kill him. Shun was accepted by Heaven and the people through his conduct and later became sovereign.

l: Yao, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Yao associated Shun with the government and presented him to Heaven and the people. Heaven and the people accepted Shun after he successfully performed sacrifices and administered affairs.

l: Gu Sou, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Gu Sou was Shun’s father and did not accord with him. Shun nevertheless honoured and nourished Gu Sou as the father of the sovereign, displaying the highest filial piety.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Confucius is cited as saying that there are not two suns in the sky or two sovereigns over the people. He is also cited on the equal righteousness of the different forms of succession under Tang, Yu, and the later rulers.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Tang sent messengers with silk three times to invite Yi Yin into his service. He accepted Yi Yin’s counsel to attack Xia and save the people.

l: Yu, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Yu was presented to Heaven by Shun and succeeded after Shun’s death when the people followed him rather than Shun’s son. Yu later presented Yi to Heaven, but after Yu’s death the people followed Qi instead of Yi.

l: Yi, Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang), Mencius, Book V (Wan Zhang) / Part I / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 7
s: Yi was presented to Heaven by Yu but did not receive the throne after Yu’s death. The princes, litigants, and singers followed Qi, Yu’s son, rather than Yi.
